# Results — Study 426 (Know Sure Thing / KST)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Martin Pring's **Know Sure Thing**
is a weighted sum of four SMA-smoothed rate-of-change series with a signal-line crossover rule.
We build it as a daily **long/flat** (and long/short) timing overlay on SPY and race its **NET
excess-of-cash Sharpe** against buy-and-hold, a 200-day SMA, and MACD — with a HAC *t*, a
sign-flip permutation placebo, a cost sweep, and a one-day execution lag. Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance SPY daily, **auto-adjusted (total return)** — public, no key |
| Window | 1993-01-29 → **2026-06-23** (as-of: last fully-closed session; the in-progress bar is dropped) |
| Bars / span | **8,406** daily bars, **33.4** years |
| Fingerprint (close) | `b7fff1b5e020` |
| Indicator | Pring daily KST: ROC (10, 15, 20, 30), SMA (10, 10, 10, 15), signal SMA 9 |
| Rule / lag / costs | long when KST > signal (else flat/short); **enter one day after** the signal (one `shift`); **1 bp** one-way × NAV per position change; shorts pay **50 bp/yr** borrow; **excess-of-cash** Sharpe both sides |

## The race — net excess Sharpe vs the simpler benchmarks

The only test that matters for a *more complicated* indicator: does it beat the obvious simpler
tools? Net of 1 bp one-way × NAV, one-day lag, excess-of-cash.

| arm | net excess Sharpe | CAGR | worst drawdown | HAC *t* | exposure | trades | turnover/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **KST (long/flat)** | **0.445** | 4.29% | −26.1% | 2.65 | 0.47 | 458 | 13.7 |
| Buy-and-hold | **0.643** | 10.76% | −55.2% | 4.33 | 1.00 | 1 | 0.0 |
| SMA-200 (Faber) | **0.727** | 8.32% | −28.3% | 4.51 | 0.75 | 215 | 6.4 |
| MACD (12,26,9) | 0.421 | 4.11% | −38.5% | 2.63 | 0.50 | 712 | 21.3 |

Read it carefully. **Every** arm clears HAC *t* = 2 on its own excess returns — including
buy-and-hold (*t* = 4.33). That is the trap: a long-only timing rule earns the **equity risk
premium** while invested, so a standalone *t* > 2 is **not** evidence of timing skill. On the
metric that actually compares strategies — risk-adjusted return — KST (**0.445**) sits **below**
buy-and-hold (**0.643**) and well below the one-line SMA-200 (**0.727**), and merely ties MACD.

## Does the timing add information? — sign-flip permutation placebo

Keep the KST exposure schedule fixed, randomise only the **direction** of each day's position
(5,000 fair coins), and ask how often a random sign-schedule matches the real one.

| | gross Sharpe | p(random ≥ observed) |
|---|--:|--:|
| KST long/flat schedule | 0.458 | **0.0044** |

The KST direction **does** beat a coin (p ≈ 0.004): there is a faint but genuine momentum signal.
This is what keeps the Signal at **WEAK** rather than **NONE** — but "beats a coin" is a far lower
bar than "beats holding the market."

## The decisive tradability test — KST minus buy-and-hold

The literal value-add of *trading* the rule over *not* trading it: the daily spread
(KST net − buy-and-hold net).

| | spread vs buy-and-hold | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| KST long/flat | **−7.16%/yr** | **−3.31** |

KST **significantly underperforms** buy-and-hold (spread *t* = −3.31). Its standalone *t* = 2.65
looked respectable, but measured as value-add over the benchmark the rule is significantly in the
red. This is the number that flips Tradability to **MIRAGE**.

## Costs are not the killer — cost sweep

| one-way cost | KST net excess Sharpe | buy-and-hold |
|---|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bp (gross) | 0.458 | 0.643 |
| 1.0 bp | 0.445 | 0.643 |
| 2.0 bp | 0.432 | 0.643 |
| 5.0 bp | 0.394 | 0.643 |

KST is below buy-and-hold even at **zero** cost — the gap is in the gross timing signal, not in
trading frictions.

## The long/short variant is a disaster

Flipping to **short** below the signal line (instead of going flat):

| | net excess Sharpe | CAGR | worst drawdown | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| KST long/short | **−0.139** | −4.22% | **−81.4%** | −0.90 |

The short leg has no edge at all — "sell" is not a tradeable signal on SPY, only "be in cash" is.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic AR(1) tape we plant **return-trend** and track the value-add (KST −
buy-and-hold spread). With no trend the spread is strongly negative (timing only sacrifices beta);
as trend rises it climbs toward zero and KST's Sharpe overtakes buy-and-hold's.

| planted trend (AR1) | KST Sharpe | buy-and-hold Sharpe | KST − BAH spread | spread *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.00 (no trend) | 0.591 | 0.732 | −5.41%/yr | −1.86 |
| +0.20 (moderate) | 0.776 | 0.775 | −3.99%/yr | −1.14 |
| +0.35 (strong) | 0.973 | 0.808 | −2.21%/yr | −0.53 |

The harness rewards trend when it exists (KST overtakes buy-and-hold at strong planted trend) and
correctly shows timing *hurts* when it doesn't. So the real-tape miss is a **true negative**: SPY
simply does not trend persistently enough for KST to add value over holding it.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The long/flat book clears HAC **t = 2.65** and beats a sign-flip coin with
  identical exposure (**p = 0.0044**), so there is a faint, *real* directional signal. But it is
  **beta in disguise**: the value-add over buy-and-hold is significantly negative (spread
  **t = −3.31**). A genuine pulse with no separable skill — WEAK, not REAL.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Net excess Sharpe KST **0.445** < buy-and-hold **0.643** < SMA-200
  **0.727**; the rule sheds **~7%/yr** versus doing nothing, even at zero cost, and the long/short
  variant is Sharpe **−0.14** at a **−81%** drawdown. Not deployable as an edge — only as a
  drawdown-cutter, and SMA-200 does that strictly better (similar −28% drawdown, 8.3% CAGR).
- **"A sure thing"? — BUSTED.** KST loses the race to **both** buy-and-hold and a one-line
  SMA-200, and only ties MACD. Pring's four-ROC machinery buys nothing the simplest trend filter
  doesn't do better. The name oversells; the indicator is, at best, an ordinary trend filter — and
  a below-average one on the US equity index.
